title: How good does a cloth simulator have to be before the laundry-robot hanger it designs is the right one?
lede: research programme: how much cloth-simulator fidelity and fabric data a laundry-robot hanger design loop needs before its choice holds on a validated solver; milestone 1, on four fabrics with published KES-FB bending rigidity and weight, finds the 2D chain and 3D sheet agree on every decision (wood-shaped hanger, arm 1 cm wider than the half shoulder) but agree to 0.004 cm because on a deep arm they are one model, and on a 3 cm arm the solver error (0.05 to 0.11 cm) is as large as the margin that picks the width (0.08 to 0.13 cm); milestone 1b solves the 3 cm arm to convergence and its best width moves to +1.5 cm on all four fabrics, against +1.0 cm in the 2D chain, a disagreement the 3000-iteration cap hid by flattering narrow arms; milestone 2a builds a simulated Cusick drape test on the 3D sheet: it orders the fabrics by bending length, but unmeasured stretch stiffness moves the drape coefficient 0.15 to 0.23 and, stiffened, every fabric drapes alike at about 0.77 (the spring grid locks), so drape cannot calibrate bending rigidity on this tier; milestone 1c reruns the 3 cm arm across stretch stiffness and mesh: the mesh leaves the width choice alone, but EA moves it from +2.0 to +2.5 cm at 40 N/m to +0.5 to +1.0 cm at 800 N/m while the 2D chain stays near +1.0 cm, so the tier disagreement changes sign with an unmeasured fabric property; milestone 2b refines the drape test's grid to 2.5 mm: the stiff suiting converges but the soft jersey does not above 150 N/m, and swapping springs shows most of the leftover stretch dependence is the shear spring the model ties to EA, a stiffness the same KES table measures (G = 26 to 89 N/m); milestone 1d sets the shear spring from measured G: stretch still moves the shallow-arm width by 1.0 cm across 40 to 800 N/m, but at 800 N/m and up, including the stiffness the KES tensile data imply, all four fabrics pick +1.0 cm, matching the 2D chain, so the tier disagreement is a soft-cloth effect and only the low-load tensile toe of the cotton jersey and shirting is left to measure; milestone 5 proves that a cheap tier's regret is bounded by how much its error varies across designs, not by its size, and finds that bound certifies no 2D-chain width (its error spreads 0.6 to 1.3 cm across widths against 0.05 to 0.25 cm margins, though the realised regret averages 0.03 cm), only a nearby stiffness guess, so the cheap tier can screen widths but not judge them; milestone 5b keeps the cheap tier's penalty term, a bound 2.8 times tighter on the 2D chain, and as a screen-and-verify loop (three reference runs around the cheap choice, then whatever the bound cannot rule out) finds the reference-tier best width in 48 of 50 tier pairs with 3.9 of 7 reference runs; milestone 3a builds ARCSim's triangle element with a Newton solver: it matches the exact cantilever elastica (within 0.9% of the overhang, extrapolated) but fails the Cusick acceptance test, locking on the soft jersey above EA 150 N/m and drifting 0.016 per refinement on the suiting; milestone 3b continues each stiff case from the soft equilibrium, all 40 converge, and at the jersey's sourced stiffness (254 and 369 N/m) the drape coefficient is flat in mesh (within 0.011) and stretch (0.003), so the jersey passes; the suiting misses by 0.004 to 0.006 through a fold-count change, and fold branches of one case differ by up to 0.32; milestone 3c runs seven seeds per case: the suiting lands in 6 to 10 folds, seed spread 0.013, and its seed-mean drape still rises 0.030 to 0.033 from 3.75 to 2.5 mm (acceptance failed by 0.0025 at 1,896 N/m), but the lower-drape branch is lower in energy in all four of 3b's discordant cases and, post hoc, the lowest-energy seed's drape coefficient moves only 0.001 to 0.009 with the mesh, so finer meshes trap more seeds in stiffer, higher-energy fold patterns; milestone 3d builds an element-local Hessian (matches the coloured finite-difference one to 8e-10, Newton steps 3x faster) and adds a 1.875 mm lattice: the registered lowest-energy-of-seven rule fails on the suiting (+0.021, an 8-fold state where 2.5 mm had a 7-fold one), the seed mean converges on both fabrics (under 0.008 from 2.5 to 1.875 mm), and a Hessian differing by under 1e-9 sends 13 of 14 chains to different fold states, so the seed and the solver's path, not the seed alone, pick the pattern; post hoc, the suiting's 7-fold pattern carried to 1.875 mm is the lowest found there and moves only +0.004; milestone 3e pools each lattice's search with the other lattices' fold patterns, and the registered lowest-energy rule then passes (+0.007 and +0.005 from 2.5 to 1.875 mm), the suiting's 7-fold pattern lowest on all three lattices; milestone 3f traces 3e's high-energy jersey transfers to the rim fill: an affine rim transfer puts 41 of 42 in the target mesh's own energy band and moves the pooled drape coefficient by at most 0.002; milestone 3g reports the drape coefficient as an interval over states within 1e-5 J of the lowest: the jersey spans 0.156 to 0.174 with no preferred state, and the interval is mesh-flat (under 0.007) for every band from 1e-5 to 3e-4 J; milestone 4a is the first comparison with real fabric: given only measured FAST data for nine wovens (Petrak et al. 2021), the uncalibrated tier ranks their measured Cusick drape coefficients with r = 0.965, above the commercial CAD simulation published with them (0.85 to 0.94), but over-drapes every fabric (bias +0.14, RMSE 0.148, acceptance failed) and is not mesh-flat at these stiffnesses; one shared factor of 0.485 on bending rigidity cuts the error to RMSE 0.050 leave-one-out; milestone 4b's orthotropic element (warp and weft bending and stretch kept apart) over-drapes slightly more (RMSE 0.161), so the factor is not the averaged-away anisotropy; milestone 4c finds the element locks: along each fabric's stretch-stiffness ladder at a fixed fold count the stretch energy falls as EA^-0.06 to EA^-0.31 instead of 1/EA, the drape coefficient climbs 0.004 to 0.015 per doubling of EA with no plateau from 18.75 N/m to the fabric's secant stiffness, and that climb is 0.044 of the 0.154 bias; a 100 gf/cm secant EA is therefore not a neutral input on this tier; milestone 4d swaps in an edge-midpoint (Crouzeix-Raviart) membrane: at the fabrics' real stiffness its stretch energy keeps falling (local exponent -0.63 to -0.91, against -0.10 to +0.30 for the locked element) and the over-drape drops by 0.030 to +0.102 (RMSE 0.107, Spearman 0.967), but the in-plane jump penalty the element needs to converge moves the drape coefficient by about 0.05 between penalty weights 0.01 and 1, as much as the locking did
summary: An open research programme on designing a laundry robot's hangers by cloth simulation: how much simulator fidelity and how much measured fabric data the design loop needs before the hanger it picks is still the best one on a validated, calibrated solver, and whether cheap models can certify that. The proposal reviews 19 works (cloth solvers, cloth parameter fitting, the cloth sim-to-real gap, multi-fidelity and robust design), states four falsifiable hypotheses and targets IEEE RA-L. Milestone 1 scores three stock hangers and five arm widths on four fabrics whose bending rigidity (0.0066 to 0.125 gf·cm²/cm) and weight are published KES-FB measurements, in three model tiers (2D chain, 3D sheet on a slab arm, 3D sheet on a 3 cm half-depth arm scored on the whole sheet). Every tier picks the wood-shaped hanger (0.38 to 0.47 cm RMS from the worn shape on the slab, against 3.1 to 3.4 cm for wire and plastic) and an arm 1 cm wider than the half shoulder on every fabric; the only ranking disagreement is a tie for second place. But on a deep arm the 2D and 3D errors differ by at most 0.004 cm, so their agreement is no test of fidelity, and on the 3 cm arm doubling the solver iterations moves the error by 0.05 to 0.11 cm, the same size as the 0.08 to 0.13 cm margin that decides the width. Milestone 1b solves those 3 cm-arm cases to convergence (12,000 to 24,000 iterations, error change under 0.002 cm per 3000). The best width moves to +1.5 cm on all four fabrics (on the 1 cm grid, +2 on fabric D), while the 2D chain stays sharply at +1.0 cm. The 3000-iteration bias depends on the width (+0.22 cm at −1 cm, −0.07 cm at +3 cm), so stopping early favoured narrow arms and made the tiers look as if they agreed. Simulation only: stretch stiffness (150 N/m) is assumed, garments are one size-M strip, there is no friction and no validated solver yet. Milestone 2a builds a simulated Cusick drape test (30 cm specimen on an 18 cm disc) on the same sheet, made isotropic in bending, and solves 140 cases to a drape-coefficient stopping rule. The drape coefficient orders the four fabrics by bending length (0.19, 0.21, 0.32, 0.45) with seed noise under 0.01, but the unmeasured stretch stiffness moves it by 0.15 to 0.23 (EA 40 against 800 N/m), shear by 0.08 to 0.11 and the mesh by up to 0.05; post hoc, stiffening the springs to 12,800 N/m lifts every fabric to about 0.77, so two fabrics with 19-fold different bending rigidity drape alike. That is membrane locking of the square spring grid: on this tier a measured drape coefficient cannot pin bending rigidity, so drape calibration moves to the validated top tier, whose first acceptance test is this one. No measured drape table could be reached this session. Milestone 1c reruns the converged 3 cm arm on fabrics A and D at EA 40, 150 and 800 N/m and two mesh changes (70 cases, all converged, predictions committed first): the mesh keeps the +1.5 cm choice, but the 3D sheet's best width goes from +2.0 to +2.5 cm at EA 40 to +0.5 to +1.0 cm at EA 800, while the 2D chain stays at +1.0 cm (+1.5 for fabric D at EA 40). The 3D-against-2D disagreement therefore runs from +1.0 to −0.5 cm with a stretch stiffness the KES-FB2 table does not give: on a shallow arm, bending rigidity and weight do not pick the hanger on this tier, and measured tensile data is a precondition for calibration. Milestone 2b refines the drape test's spring grid from 7.5 to 2.5 mm (26 cases, predictions committed first). The stiff suiting converges to about 0.01, but the soft jersey does not at EA 800 N/m and up (0.70 to 0.37 at EA 3200, still falling), and the overhang barely compresses at any EA (under 0.15%). A post hoc swap shows the sheet's shear spring, tied to EA at 0.1, carries most of the leftover dependence: on the suiting at 2.5 mm, shear alone (80 to 320 N/m) raises DC by 0.046 and stretch alone (800 to 3200 N/m) by 0.027; on the jersey, 0.139 against 0.013. Shear rigidity is measured in the same KES table as B and W (G = 0.47 to 1.58 gf/cm/deg, 26 to 89 N/m per radian), so it can now be set from data; the shallow-arm width shift of milestone 1c uses the same coupling and is the next thing to recheck. Milestone 1d reruns that shallow-arm choice with the shear spring set from each fabric's measured G and stretch stiffness swept on its own (126 converged cases, 4 fabrics). Shear was a third of milestone 1c's effect: EA 40 to 800 N/m still moves the best width by 1.0 cm (+2.0 to +1.0) on both the jersey and the suiting. But from 800 N/m up, including a secant stiffness derived from the same table's tensile LT and WT (2,360 to 15,490 N/m, assuming the standard 500 gf/cm load), every fabric picks +1.0 cm, the 2D chain's answer, with every margin certified by the stopping rule. So the 3D-against-2D disagreement is a soft-cloth effect. A post hoc power-law fit to LT and WT puts the suiting and the elastane jersey well inside the settled regime at the garment's own shoulder load (tangent 1,300 to 6,200 N/m), but the cotton jersey (250 to 370 N/m) and the shirting (700 to 1,050 N/m) in the band where the choice flips. Settling them needs the low-load toe of the tensile curve, not the KES summary numbers. Milestone 5 proves the planned margin bound: the reference-tier regret of a cheap tier’s choice is at most the spread of the paired tier error across designs (max e − min e), not its size, and a choice is certified when the cheap tier’s margin exceeds that spread (or a Lipschitz cone of it). On the 50 tier pairs milestones 1b to 1d recorded, the 2D chain’s error against the 3D sheet (up to 1.6 to 2.0 cm) spreads 0.6 to 1.3 cm across widths, ten times the chain’s margins, so no 2D choice is certified even though its realised regret is small (mean 0.03 cm, at most 0.20 cm); only a stretch-stiffness guess of 3200 N/m against the KES-sourced value is certified (2 or 3 of 4 fabrics). The cheap tier screens out a median 3 of 7 widths but cannot judge the rest; the reference tier is still our own sheet, not a validated solver. Milestone 5b keeps the cheap tier’s own penalty: the regret is at most maxd [K |d − d̂| − (st(d) − st(d̂))], with K the slope of the paired error around the choice. On the 2D chain the realised regret is a median 34% of that bound against 12% of milestone 5’s; with K estimated from three reference runs it covers the regret in 47 of 50 tier pairs (all 50 with K doubled). A screen-and-verify loop built on it finds the reference optimum in 48 of 50 pairs with 3.9 of 7 reference runs (mean regret 0.0010 cm against 0.0022 for the best of the three runs and 0.028 for trusting the cheap tier); its two misses are the softest cloth (EA 40 N/m), whose optimum is two grid steps from the cheap choice. Milestone 3a writes ARCSim’s element model (constant-strain triangles with stretch and measured KES shear as separate parameters, discrete-shell hinge bending, a Newton solver with a coloured finite-difference Hessian) as a candidate top tier. It matches the exact heavy-cantilever elastica (the basis of ASTM D1388’s 41.5° rule) to within 0.9% of the overhang after first-order extrapolation, and stretch stiffness moves the cantilever by under 0.31%. But it fails the simulated Cusick acceptance test: on the suiting the drape coefficient still climbs about 0.016 per mesh refinement and 0.034 from EA 800 to 3200 N/m (40% less than the spring sheet), and on the soft jersey it converges only at EA 150 N/m, near the jersey’s sourced tangent stiffness, and locks above it, so constant-strain triangles are not the top tier. Milestone 3b continues each stiff case from the soft equilibrium instead of a cold start: all 40 cases converge, and at the jersey’s own sourced tangent stiffness (254 and 369 N/m) the drape coefficient moves by only 0.008 to 0.011 from a 3.75 to a 2.5 mm lattice and by 0.003 from 150 to 369 N/m, so 3a’s jersey “locking” was mostly unconverged solves, and the element passes the acceptance test there. The suiting at its sourced 1,341 and 1,896 N/m misses the 0.03 mesh bar by 0.004 to 0.006 through a change from 6 to 7 folds, and the same case can settle in fold patterns whose drape coefficients differ by up to 0.32, so calibration against a measured drape will need the measured node count too. Milestone 3c runs seven seeds per case (98 stages, all converged): on the suiting at 1,896 N/m and 2.5 mm the seeds land in 7, 8, 9 and 10 folds, with a seed spread of 0.013 in drape coefficient, four-fifths of it explained by the fold count; the seed-mean drape coefficient still rises 0.030 and 0.033 from 3.75 to 2.5 mm at the suiting’s two sourced stiffnesses (Welch standard error 0.007), so the revised acceptance fails by 0.0025 at 1,896 N/m, while the jersey passes again (−0.008, −0.010). In all four of 3b’s discordant cases the lower-drape fold pattern has the lower energy, and, post hoc, the lowest-energy of the seven seeds moves by only 0.001 to 0.009 between the two meshes on both fabrics: the suiting’s mesh dependence is finer meshes trapping more starts in stiffer, higher-energy fold patterns, not a drift of the minimum. Two of 106 end states had a negative smallest eigenvalue; one is a genuine saddle that descends to a softer pattern, the other a flat direction worth 1.6×10−8 J. Milestone 3d replaces the solver’s coloured finite-difference Hessian (120 gradient calls per Newton step) with element blocks, exact for the membrane: it agrees to 8×10−10 and makes Newton steps 2.98 times faster, enough for a third lattice (1.875 mm, 23,509 nodes). The lowest-energy-of-seven rule, registered before the run, fails on the suiting: its drape coefficient moves +0.021 from 2.5 to 1.875 mm, because no seed found the 7-fold pattern there; the jersey passes (+0.006). The seed mean converges on both fabrics (under 0.008 from 2.5 to 1.875 mm, against the suiting’s +0.033 one step coarser). And with the same starts, the new Hessian, different by under 10−9, sent 13 of 14 chains to different fold states at 3.75 mm, with seed means within 0.005: the fold pattern is picked by the seed and the solver’s rounding together, so the seed mean, not the lowest of a few seeds, is the summary to calibrate against a measured drape. Post hoc, the suiting’s 7-fold pattern carried from 2.5 to 1.875 mm stays 7-fold, is lower in energy than all seven 1.875 mm seeds and moves the drape coefficient by only +0.004: the rule failed by sampling, not because the lowest pattern moved. Milestone 3e pools the search on one solver: each lattice also re-solves the fold patterns every other lattice found. The registered lowest-energy rule then passes, moving +0.007 (jersey) and +0.005 (suiting) from 2.5 to 1.875 mm, and the suiting’s 7-fold pattern is the lowest state on all three lattices. The one-solver seed mean also converges (under 0.006), but on the suiting it sits 0.026 above that pattern (8 to 10 folds against 7), so a measured node count will decide which summary a real Cusick test matches. Milestone 3f traces 3e’s high-energy jersey transfers to how the transfer filled the cloth’s rim: continuing the rim along the cloth’s own tangent plane puts 41 of 42 transfers inside the target mesh’s own energy band (worst 2.3×10−5 J above it, against 6.4×10−4 J), and the pooled drape coefficient moves by at most 0.002; the registered acceptance still fails on one transfer that stops at the step cap, and the jersey’s mesh margin shrinks to 0.0005 under the 0.01 bar. Milestone 3g reports the drape coefficient as an interval over every distinct state within 10−5 J of the lowest (the work of lowering the overhang by 0.1 to 0.2 mm): the jersey’s 20 or so states per mesh all lie within 3×10−5 J, so its drape coefficient is an interval about 0.016 wide (0.156 to 0.174), the suiting’s 7-fold pattern is lowest with an 8-fold one at the band edge, and the interval’s midpoint moves under 0.007 between the two finest meshes for every band from 10−5 to 3×10−4 J, which a single lowest state does not. Milestone 4a is the first comparison with real fabric: nine woven fabrics with measured FAST and KES-FB data and a measured Cusick drape coefficient on the same geometry (Petrak et al. 2021, Materials 14, 6259, CC BY). Given only those inputs and no fitted parameter, the triangle-FEM tier orders the nine fabrics almost exactly as measured (Pearson 0.965, Spearman 0.967, above every column of the commercial CAD simulation published with the data, 0.85 to 0.94), but it over-drapes every one by 0.09 to 0.20 (RMSE 0.148 against a registered bar of 0.08), and at these stretch stiffnesses (1,800 to 4,800 N/m) the drape coefficient still rises by about 0.03 from the 3.75 to the 2.5 mm mesh. KES bending in place of FAST removes the bias but scatters the fabrics (r 0.65). Post hoc, one shared factor of 0.485 on FAST bending rigidity predicts each held-out fabric with RMSE 0.050, and solved at that factor the tier matches all nine to RMSE 0.036 (in-sample): on this tier calibration is necessary, and one parameter is enough for these wovens. Milestone 4b keeps warp and weft apart (bending up to 4:1, stretch up to 11:1) in an orthotropic element calibrated to be exact on both axes: it over-drapes slightly more (bias +0.152, RMSE 0.161, r 0.919), because the hinge lattice's off-axis bending is 1.0 to 1.6 times the geometric mean, so the 0.485 factor is not the averaged-away anisotropy; one-seed model differences under about 0.01 are fold-state noise. Milestone 4c tests the next suspect, membrane locking, on the same element: rebuilt to reproduce 4a's 96 logged stages exactly, each fabric's stretch-stiffness ladder at a fixed fold count shows the stretch energy falling as EA−0.06 to EA−0.31 (locking-free: EA−1), the drape coefficient rising in 39 of 39 steps (0.004 to 0.015 per doubling, no plateau), and the climb from 150 N/m to the secant EA averaging +0.044 of the +0.154 seed-0 bias. Lowering EA to 18.75 N/m cuts the bias to +0.045 (RMSE 0.057) but the EA that would match each fabric, extrapolated, runs from 0.01 to 23 N/m, so stretch is not one calibration knob; refining the mesh from 3.75 to 2.5 mm does not reduce the climb, which fits the constraint count of linear triangles (four inextensibility constraints per node against three degrees of freedom). Milestone 4d replaces the membrane with an edge-midpoint (Crouzeix–Raviart) element after English and Bridson (2008), stabilised by a penalty on the in-plane jump across each edge (without it the free rim has zero-energy modes and Newton stalls). At the top of each ladder the stretch energy now keeps falling (local exponent −0.63 to −0.91; conforming −0.10 to +0.30) and the drape coefficient rises 0.0005 to 0.0067 per doubling (conforming 0.005 to 0.011), but over the whole ladder from 150 N/m the registered locking-free bar fails (exponent −0.48 to −0.80). The bias at the secant EA falls from +0.133 to +0.102 on the 3.75 mm lattice (RMSE 0.137 to 0.107, Spearman 0.967 unchanged), less than the 0.044 4c forecast, and the penalty weight, a numerical parameter, moves the drape coefficient by 0.048 on average between 0.01 and 1 (0.059 on 5 mm), so the remaining bias cannot be quoted without it.
